good.rex: Second attempt took. Joint reduced, sling on. The casualty's language was within regulations. Mostly.
good.chip: Reduced on attempt two! MediRight™ notes that unindexed words are not covered by your plan!
good.ajoy: Second go, but it's in. The first pull was a little quick. The sling's on, so I'll let that go. Mostly.

poor.aria: It wouldn't go back in, so the arm's strapped and resting. It'll settle the slow way. I'm sorry it hurt so much.
poor.marv: The muscles clamped too hard. Arm strapped as it is. It will reset on its own schedule, which is slower than ours.
poor.rex: Reduction failed. Arm immobilised as it lies. Slow recovery. The whole crew heard every attempt.
poor.chip: Reduction unsuccessful. MediRight™ has moved the patient to the Slow Way recovery plan. No upsell today.
poor.ajoy: It didn't go. Too late and a little quick, which I did mention. It's strapped, and it'll settle on its own.

fedup.aria: They've had enough and walked off with the arm strapped. That's okay. It'll settle the slow way.
fedup.marv: The patient declined further attempts and left, arm strapped as it is. A reasonable position, frankly.
fedup.rex: Casualty withdrew from treatment. Arm strapped where it sits. Slow recovery. Their call to make.
fedup.chip: The patient has opted out of treatment. MediRight™ respects your crew's right to decline further attempts.
fedup.ajoy: They walked out, arm strapped. After that many attempts I can't say I blame them. It'll settle on its own.

perfect.narrative: A slow, steady pull, a long breath out, and the shoulder slides home with a soft clunk everyone feels in their teeth. The colour is back in the patient's face before the sling goes on. The diagram, it turns out, was right to be cheerful.

good.narrative: It takes a long minute and a second go, but the joint goes back where it belongs. The patient says a word the manual doesn't index. The sling goes on, and the mending starts.

poor.narrative: The muscles have clamped too hard. Attempt follows attempt, and the patient goes greyer with each, until you stop and strap the arm as it is. It will settle back eventually, the slow way. Everyone aboard heard every attempt.

outcome.narrative: {crew.medic} lays the patient face down on the galley table with the arm hanging over the edge and a full water bottle taped to the wrist, then waits, talking about nothing, while gravity does the arguing. After a while the muscles tire, the shoulder slips back in on its own, and the medic looks as if this was always the plan. It was.

choices.text: Muscle relaxant from a medkit, then try

outcome.narrative: The medkit's muscle relaxant does what persuasion couldn't. A little while later the shoulder goes back in with almost no argument, and the patient falls asleep in the middle of saying thank you.

choices.text: Sling it and leave it for a station

outcome.narrative: You strap the arm across the chest and leave the joint for someone with an X-ray. The patient is brave about it at every bump, every hatch and every attempt to sleep. Brave is tiring. Everyone gets tired.

science_link.text: One old way to put a shoulder back: lay the patient face down with the arm hanging and a weight at the wrist, and let tired muscles do the rest. It's called the Stimson technique.
science_link.label: Dislocated shoulder

title: Covering the Shift

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has volunteered to cover the shift! ARIA has been reminded she can't hold a wrench! ARIA has volunteered to hold the clipboard!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV can cover the station. MARV will do it exactly as written. MARV has read what is written. MARV recommends someone else reads it before he starts.
ai_flavor.rex: REX does not leave a post unmanned. He has stood at the empty station for an hour. He has not touched anything. The post is, technically, manned.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP offers ShiftCover™ automated staffing at no extra charge! The charge is in fuel! CHIP is legally required to call that no extra charge!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says they will rest when they believe the job is handled. Handle it any way you like, and say so out loud. Muttering it doesn't count.

body:
Someone in the crew is hurt, and their job did not get the memo.

The work is still there: the checks, the logs, the small daily jobs that keep a ship a ship. Their station sits empty, lights blinking politely. The patient keeps trying to get up to see to it. The patient keeps being told to lie down. Both of these keep happening.

Someone has to cover. Every someone has a price.

outcome.narrative: You take their station on top of your own and do both badly enough to be honest about it. Everything aboard runs a little late. The patient, finally convinced the job is in someone's hands, sleeps properly for the first time since it happened, and the healing gets on with itself.

choices.text: Hand it to the ship computer

outcome.narrative: The ship computer takes over their station and runs it by the manual, which was written for a ship with more fuel than this one and errs on the side of burning it. The job gets done. The patient rests. The fuel gauge carries the cost quietly.

choices.text: Let them run it from the bunk

outcome.narrative: You run a cable to the bunk and a screen to the patient. They work their station lying down, cheerful and useful and healing at the speed of someone who is still working. Nobody can call it a bad idea to their face.

title: Can't Sleep

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has been singing the patient a lullaby! In text! On the ceiling screen! It has not helped! It has been very pretty!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has measured the drive's hum in sick bay. It sits exactly where a human ear finds it hardest to ignore. MARV did not design the ship. MARV would like that noted.
ai_flavor.rex: REX can sleep anywhere. He once slept through a hull breach. He does not understand the problem. He has stopped offering his method, which is exhaustion.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP recommends the DreamPod™ sleep capsule! It is soundproofed, heated and very comfortable! It is also on the cancelled-features list, right after the second bathroom!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has dimmed sick bay and muted the alerts. It's the drive. Move them, stop it or dose them. She'd have put the cot somewhere else in the first place.

body:
The patient can't sleep.

It isn't the pain, exactly, or not only. The sick bay cot sits against the bulkhead nearest the drive, and the drive hums all night in a key that gets into the bones, and the bones in question are already having a hard week. They lie awake counting the rivets in the ceiling. They know all of them now.

Most healing happens during sleep. This patient has been doing very little of either.

choices.text: Move their cot into the growbay

outcome.narrative: You move the cot between the planters and dim the lamps to night for them. The growbay is the quietest room aboard, warm and damp and smelling of soil, and the patient is asleep inside the hour. The crop loses its nights of full light and shows it. The patient wakes up better, and talking to the plants.

choices.text: Cut the drive and drift for a night

outcome.narrative: You shut the drive down after dinner and let the ship coast through the dark in silence. The patient is asleep before the hum has finished fading and sleeps clean through to the restart. The schedule loses the night. The patient gets it.
A measured dose from the medkit, and the drive's hum becomes somebody else's problem. The patient sleeps the long, flat sleep of the chemically excused and wakes stiff, groggy and visibly mended.
Nobody gets used to it. The patient spends the nights learning the ceiling and the days yawning through a recovery that drags. By the end, the rivets are a personal matter.

title: Lodged

ai_flavor.aria: We have a new part! ARIA didn't order it! ARIA is calling it a gift!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV puts the object's mass at roughly that of a vending machine, mounted off-centre. The thrusters are correcting for it on every burn. MARV can do this all day. The fuel cannot.
ai_flavor.rex: REX wants to know whose it is. If it's theirs, it's a trophy. If it's ours, it's evidence. Either way he wants it inside.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is thrilled to announce the ship has an aftermarket accessory! It was not fitted by an authorised dealer! It voids the warranty in a whole new place!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says it's good metal if someone goes out for it, and a slow fuel leak if nobody does. A hard burn shakes it free and takes some plating with it. She listed the spacewalk first for a reason.

body:
After the fight, the hull sensors report something new: a lump.

A piece of something, the other ship's or a stray round's or nobody's, has punched into the outer plating aft and stuck there, half in and half out, like a dart that missed the board and hit the wall. It hasn't gone through. It is heavy. Every time the drive fires, the ship pulls very slightly to one side, and the thrusters spend fuel pulling it back.

choices.text: Cut it out and keep the metal

outcome.narrative: A spacewalk, a cutting torch and a long, careful afternoon. The lump comes free and comes inside, where it turns out to be good metal that someone else paid for. It leaves a hole behind, which is the thing about holes. You patch it as well as a patch can.

choices.text: {crew.engineer} pulls it and plates the hole

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} goes out with the torch and comes back with the lump, then goes out again with plate and sealant and does the hole properly, stronger than the panel around it. The ship flies straight. The engineer sits in the airlock for a while afterwards with their helmet off, looking pleased.

You leave it. It stays, a souvenir nobody wanted, and on every burn for the rest of the leg the thrusters lean against it. The fuel spent keeping the ship straight adds up quietly, the way small leans do.

choices.text: Shake it loose with a hard burn

outcome.narrative: You fire the drive hard and cut it, then again, like a dog shaking off water. On the second jolt the lump tears free and tumbles away into the dark. It takes a strip of plating with it, as a keepsake.

title: Everything in the Growbay Moved

ai_flavor.aria: The crop went on a ROLLERCOASTER! ARIA thinks it had a great time! ARIA has looked at its readings! ARIA has stopped thinking that!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has checked the fight's manoeuvres against the growbay's tie-down procedure. There was no tie-down procedure. MARV has now written one. It is very short and would have taken a minute.
ai_flavor.rex: REX takes responsibility for the hard turns. He would take them again. Next time he will strap the planters down first.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that GroTray™ planters are rated for gentle cruising! CHIP has checked! A space battle is not gentle cruising! CHIP has updated the definition!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says roots in the air first; they dry fastest. The glass will hold a little while, and the plants that only look bad can wait. Strapping them down was also an option. Earlier.

body:
Nobody thought to strap down the growbay before the fight.

Every hard turn and every hit has been redistributed through the planters. There is soil on the walls. A tray of seedlings is upside down in the corner, looking surprised. The {crop.name} is still in its beds, mostly, at angles it did not choose, roots half out and leaves pressed flat against the glass, and one glass panel has a crack across it.

It is alive. It would like someone to come in.

choices.text: Scoop it all back by hand

outcome.narrative: Scoop by scoop the soil goes back in the beds, the roots go back under the soil, and the upturned tray is turned the right way up and forgiven. It takes the rest of the day. By evening the bay looks like a growbay again, and the plants have stopped leaning.

{crew.botanist} walks the bay once without touching anything, then fixes the plants in the order that matters: roots in the air first, the ones that only look bad last. It goes quickly, because it goes in the right order. The upturned tray turns out to have been fine. Only its soil was upside down.

You seal the cracked panel before anything else, because cracks spread and plants don't. It's a good seal. By the time you get to the beds, some of the roots that spent the afternoon in the air have dried past saving.

You close the door on the mess and see to the rest of the ship first. By the time anyone gets back to the growbay the exposed roots have dried and the leaves crushed against the glass have browned. Alive, still. Less of it.

title: The Letter Home

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has unticked the survey box! It keeps ticking itself again! ARIA is going to keep unticking it for as long as it takes!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has read the template. Every sentence in it is true, and none of it is about anyone. MARV did not know that was possible. He has learned something today he would rather not have.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has written these. Where he served, the commanding officer writes them by hand. It is the worst part of the job. It is supposed to be.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has switched off the notification survey! CHIP has never switched off a survey! CHIP does not care what it does to the metrics! This one is off!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has their record open, and the small things the log remembers that a record doesn't. She would not use the template. She'll read any of it out if it helps, and keep her other opinions for later.

body:
The next relay is close enough to send a message home, and there is a message that has to be sent.

Colonial Personnel Services has already provided a template. It arrived within the hour, which is the fastest anything from Colonial Personnel Services has ever arrived. It is warm the way a hand dryer is warm. It has a field for the name, a field for the date, and a box, ticked by default, for a short survey about the notification experience.

Somebody, somewhere, is going to read whatever goes out. It should be something worth reading.

log_lore.title: THE LETTER
log_lore.text:
To their family,

You will have had the official notice by now. This is the other one.

They were good at the work, and better at the parts of it nobody counts: knowing when someone needed a hand before they asked, fixing the thing on the list nobody else understood, laughing at the right moment and sometimes at the wrong one, which usually turned out to be the right one too.

The ship runs a little differently without them. We notice it every day. We are carrying on, because they would have been annoyed with us if we didn't, and because they believed in where we are going more loudly than most.

They were part of a crew, and the crew was better for it. I wanted you to know that most of all.

The Captain

outcome.narrative: You untick the box and start from nothing. It takes most of a day and more drafts than you'll admit to, and the last one is the shortest. It says what they did aboard, what they were like to work beside, and the story they would have wanted told. It goes out at the relay. You keep a copy in the log, because someone should.

You pass the screen round the galley table. Each person writes a line and passes it on without reading the others. Some are funny. One is only their nickname, spelled the way only a friend would spell it. The message goes out at the relay looking as if it was written by a crew, which it was.

{crew.diplomat} has written this letter before, in a different job, more often than anyone should. The draft arrives within the hour, in plain words, and it is exactly right. The diplomat asks for it to go out under your name. You send it under both.

You fill in the name and the date and send it as issued, survey and all. It is correct. It is on time. Somewhere a family will open a message from a ship and find a form, and aboard the ship, whenever the relay comes up, someone changes the subject.

title: Crew Member B

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA can be Crew Member B! ARIA has no hands! ARIA has enthusiasm! The checklist does not have a box for enthusiasm!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has checked who wrote the checklist. A committee, for a full crew. MARV notes that this ship currently has neither.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has run worse drills alone. He recommends running. He recommends running faster than you think you can.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP is delighted to offer Crew Member B™ as a subscription! It is the ship computer! It is already aboard! The subscription is for the signature!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has timed the corridor. Done properly, it's a long run. The computer is quicker and not gentle. Skipping it isn't free; it's just billed later.

body:
Today's maintenance checklist has a two-person job on it.

The coolant loop needs bleeding, which means a valve at the front of the ship held open while a valve at the back is turned, slowly, by someone else. The checklist calls them Crew Member A and Crew Member B, and gives them a signature line each. The crew roster has one name on it, and it's yours.

The valves are a long corridor apart. The checklist does not care.

outcome.narrative: You tie the front valve open with a sock, run the length of the ship, turn the back valve a notch, run back to check the front, and run back again. Somewhere in the middle of it the loop gives up its air with a gurgle and the drive temperature drops. You sign the checklist as Crew Member A, then again, more slowly, as Crew Member B. The handwriting doesn't match. You were very tired by then.

choices.text: Let the ship computer be Crew Member B

outcome.narrative: The ship computer turns the back valve with a maintenance arm built for lifting crates, not for subtlety. It turns it all the way, at once, and the loop bangs like a dropped pan and cracks a bracket. The air is out. So, briefly, was your heart. The computer signs as Crew Member B in a perfect font.

Nobody's checking. The loop keeps its air bubble, the drive runs a little hot, and running hot it burns a little more for the same push, leg after leg. The item stays open on the checklist, its signature lines empty, waiting.
